And the palm, as the gloss touches upon over the Psalm <note>a reference to Psalm 92:12 "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree"</note>, is a tree of great height; but yet it does not reach to the height of a cedar, whose root is rough and round, very fixed in the depth of the earth. Its trunk, however, is leafy and compact and of incorruptible strength. Its bark upon the trunk is hard and rugose and in some way stinging, and most especially towards the earth, and therefore it is difficult to climb, and with difficulty one arrives at its fruit. Its leaves have a pyramidal form in the manner of a sword. Although, however, the palm is hard around the stem and rough in the upper parts, yet it is of joyful aspect in the beauty of its branches, and in the crown at the summit of the branches it carries its fruits and not in the middle of the leaves, as Pliny says, book 13, whose fruit is so much the more unctuous, sweeter, and more digestive the more immediately it approaches the rays of the sun. It grows in many regions, but it does not fruit as it does in the region scorched by the spikes of the sun, in level, sandy, and vitreous soil; and therefore the palm of Judea is renowned, as Pliny says, book 13, chapter 5. Item, in the same place, the species of palms is twofold: male and female. The male flowers first, the female afterwards bursts forth into the germ; nor does the female fruit unless it is so near to the male that at least the wind mediates and the female is impregnated by the scent of the male. In the same place, the Philosopher says in his book of <term>Vegetables</term> <note>refers to Aristotle's De Plantis</note>, that when it is sown, it is necessary that the seeds of male and female be sown together, and the female should be composed two by two, and from the individuals the plant erupts, whence four plantlets coalesce from them, which cohere so much to each other and bind themselves mutually by a wondrous artifice of nature in the manner of a net. Nor does the female grow well, nor even fruit without the male; nay, if the male tree is cut down, the female after two years becomes sterile. But with the rough leaves and flowers of the male around the roots of the female, the female receives and resumes strength again as if from intercourse by the proximity of the male. Nor do such plantings like a place that is humid, fat, and smoky, but rather a place that is salty and sandy, and therefore where there is no such soil, it is necessary that salt be sprinkled, not near the root, but somewhat in the vicinity, so that by such saltiness the superfluity of the humors of the earth is consumed; and Pliny says there is a certain species of palm in the meridian, it is believed to be one, and no other is multiplied from it, but when by age it completely perishes and fails, it is born again from itself and revives, and therefore it is said that the phoenix, the bird of Arabia, received its name from the shrub of this plant or palm, because when it dies, it is said to revive, as Pliny says in the same place. Item, in the same place, the author says there are different species of palms in Ethiopia, marvelous not so much for greenness as for sweetness and for juice and speed; for their fruits are most rich in juice, whence also the best wine is expressed from them, up to here Pliny, book 18, chapter 5. The palm is therefore a singular tree, slender in the stem and hairy, in respect to the leaf from which it exits, but beautiful and dilated in the branches and foliage in respect to the heaven, to which it extends itself at its summit. Its leaves are long, in surface indeed small and thick and flexible, for various connections, being very suitable for baskets, as Jerome says; nevertheless, in the lateral angles they are incisive and sharp. Its branches are called <term>elate</term> <gloss>branches/raised things</gloss>, that is, raising themselves upward, keeping a continuous greenness, and never inclining themselves from the lowest. And according to this, the middle of this division of <term>elate</term> in the penultimate has it long, as Canticles 5 says: "Your hair is like the palm tree." <note>original: "Come tua elate palmarum"</note>. Elate, however, or <term>elates</term> in Greek is called <term>abies</term> <gloss>fir tree</gloss> in Latin, and according to this, the penultimate is shortened, and thus it seems to place another text which says in Canticles 5: "His hair as a fir tree" <note>original: "crines eius sicut abies"</note>, as the author says, and thus the middle has to be shortened, not lengthened; however, the fruit of the palm is varied as much in form as in virtue, according to the diversity of the wood from which it exits, and according to the diversity of the soil in which the palm grows, and according to the various reception of celestial heat which diffuses itself in diverse ways according to the diverse sites to the summits of the palms, as Pliny says, book 13. The first is clear, for in many palms, fruit is rarely or never found because of the bad or less than sufficient disposition of the tree itself, as is evident in Italian palms in which rarely or never is any fruit found; and if it grows, it is never found to reach maturity and due completion, as Pliny says. The second is clear from what was said before, why in soil or earth that is too cold and humid, fat or smoky and easy, they do not succeed, nay, they do not grow at all by any remedy, as the same author says. The third is also evident, that in shady places, removed from the presence of the rays of the sun, palms cannot grow; and if by chance they have grown elsewhere, they can in no way reach the glory of palms by fruiting. And this is what Plato <note>again, likely a general attribution to medical/philosophical authority</note> touches upon in the <term>Diet</term>. Dates, he says, that is, palm-bearing fruits, are cold and humid in the second degree, and have diverse actions according to the various qualities of the regions. For some are born in a cold region, that is, remotely cold; some in a hot one; some, however, in between these, temperate. Those, however, in a hot region, where there is continuous fruit, are very sweet in taste and by some viscosity somewhat unctuous, and yet, since they are very sweet, if anyone uses them too much, they cause obstructions and opilations of the stomach and also of the head, and of the pathways of the spleen and liver, from which it is evident that it is not good to use all sweet things continuously; nay, it is more often harmful to the soul and body. ### The Heart of Secrets

...other creatures were in service to that creature <note>Refers to humanity, created in God's image as discussed on the previous page.</note>; and thus He gave them a soul such as no other creature possesses, containing all the powers that no other soul has: this soul has even more, for it has a power like that of the angels; it is a **rational soul** <term>rational soul: in medieval thought, the part of the human soul capable of logic and understanding, distinguishing humans from "sensitive" animal souls</term> and yet it is a corporeal beast. It is a great thing that an earthly beast has a rational soul which possesses reason and understanding. This soul is perpetual, so that it shall never die and will always endure. But it is not so with the human body: for it is corruptible, just like the elements from which the body is made. Although *Aristotle* said that generation was perpetual <note>original: "generation estoit perpetuelle." Aristotle argued that while individuals die, the cycle of birth and decay (generation) in the sublunary world is eternal.</note>, this referred to that "generating generation" which is not itself engendered but created—that is to say, commanded. For he says that if God the Creator had destroyed all beasts, each of the parts would return to the element from which it was made. And if He broke apart the elements, they would return to ash. And that ash would, by its nature, produce parts where one is heavier than the other. This thing is done by the will of the Creator and at His command. He meant this regarding creatures of both kinds, because the elements neither grow nor diminish; we will make his meaning more clearly understood to you another time.

Of the souls of men who are endowed with reason and are perpetual, we will speak to you at greater length another time; but we must return to our first subject. Among these things, God made other corporeal things that are called clouds, and yet they are not "animated" <note>Meaning they do not possess a "soul" or life-force like animals or plants.</note>; rather, they are moved through the air by the vapors which are engendered from the sea and the earth by the force of fire and the sun. These vapors are called winds, and they come from the four parts of the world. Each of those which come from the four parts of the world are called **principal winds**, and the ancients gave them principal and proper names, just as we will tell you another time. And they are "principal" because each of these winds has two other winds coming at its side <note>This refers to the classical 12-wind rose: four cardinal winds, each flanked by two collateral winds.</note>. These winds were named (not by the common people). Of the winds, the clouds, their natures, and their powers, we shall treat more at leisure hereafter and in proper order, as it is now necessary for us to return to giving you this answer.

The Creator did one thing when He made that creature which is called the sun: for in making the sun, He made the **day**. And I shall tell you how and for what reason. First, it is necessary to know what "day" is: for day is only the clarity and the glow of the sun. For I tell you—and do not marvel at this—that nothing in the world has brightness, neither fire, nor moon, nor star, except from the sun; and we will speak of this more clearly hereafter. Now listen and accept what I tell you. I tell you that God the Creator made the day bright and shining of itself; and all other things are obscure and dark of themselves. But they receive brightness from the sun, just as I have told you before regarding the **mirror**, which has no brightness except for as much as the day gives it. So it is that the sun and the moon have an established path in the firmament <term>firmament: the sphere of the heavens or the sky</term> which we can see. And that path the astronomers call the **zodiac**; and it is this path which we imagine...

<summary>This page defines the "rational soul" as the unique, eternal trait of humanity and discusses the Aristotelian view of elements and generation. It then explains the origin of winds from vapors and identifies the sun as the sole source of light for all other celestial bodies and the creator of "day."</summary>

(The Origin of Musical Melodies)

What brought about melodies is an instinctive human nature. Among them is the poetic form, which is instinctive to humans and embedded in them from their very beginning. Among them is the animal instinct through which it vocalizes during certain pleasurable or harmful conditions. Among them is the human's love for rest after fatigue, or not feeling fatigue during work, for humming is something that distracts from fatigue during work so that it is not felt. For this reason, one does not perceive the time during which one performs a task, does not grow weary of it, and persists in it more. For the perception of time is followed by a stronger imagining of fatigue, which makes one feel it, since fatigue only follows movement, and time is a concomitant of movement. Then each of them follows the other, I mean time and movement, for neither is ever separated from the other.

It is also thought that humming might act in the same way on some other animals.

### Sultana Sauce.

Place in a saucepan a pint of broth with a glass of white wine, two slices of lemon with the peel removed, two cloves, a clove of garlic, half a bay leaf, parsley, scallions, an onion, and a root vegetable. Boil for an hour and a half over a low fire and reduce to the consistency of a sauce. Pass it through a sieve, then add a little salt, coarse pepper, a chopped hard-boiled egg yolk, and a pinch of very finely chopped blanched parsley.

### German Sauce.

Place in a saucepan a little <term>coulis</term> with an equal amount of broth, a pinch of chopped blanched parsley, two cooked poultry livers, an anchovy, and some capers, all chopped very finely. Add good butter the size of half an egg, salt, and coarse pepper. Bind the sauce over the fire and serve it as you see fit.

### English Sauce.

Chop two hard-boiled egg yolks. Place half in a saucepan with an anchovy and chopped capers, a glass of good broth, a little salt, and coarse pepper. Add butter the size of half an egg mixed with a pinch of flour. Bind the sauce over the fire. Arrange it over whatever you wish and scatter the remaining chopped egg yolk over the meat. This sauce is good for masking entrées that lack an appealing appearance.

# The Suppressing Slide (Yi)

-><gloss>In musical scores, written as "Rising"</gloss><- <note>original: 卬 (*ang*). This abbreviated character is the standard shorthand used in Guqin tablature to represent the *Yi* (抑) technique.</note>

->This refers to the act of pressing the finger down firmly to "suppress" the string while sliding it either upward or downward to a new pitch.<-

<note>The metaphor of the **Swallow Chasing Flying Insects** (*Yan zhu fei chong shi*) captures the agile and predatory precision required for this movement. Just as a swallow must be both swift and remarkably accurate to catch a flying insect mid-air, the musician’s fingers must maintain a firm, constant pressure (*Yi*) against the string while moving rapidly between positions. This ensures that the "voice" of the instrument does not flicker or fade during the slide.</note>

<term>Yi (抑): To press down, suppress, or restrain. In this musical context, it describes a slide performed with deliberate pressure to maintain a strong, clear tone throughout the pitch change.</term>

## *On investigating the distribution of vessels, ureters, and nerves in the kidneys.*
### Chapter XLIII.

Once these procedures have been correctly and properly performed, it will be the right time to follow the kidney's own <term>tunica: a natural covering or coat of an organ</term> with your scalpel. This membrane should already be pulled back and stripped away. Use one hand to grasp the <term>emulgent: an old term for the renal vessels</term> vessels, the urinary vessel <note>the ureter</note>, and the nerves that you previously tied. Follow where the scalpel leads you. This membrane is a single and continuous structure. It passes through along with these vessels and expands within the fissure. This occurs in the concave region of the kidneys where the substance appears divided and loosened on both sides. This area is quite large and penetrates deeply. As soon as the membrane is pulled back, it reveals an abundance of fat. The amount of fat present is always determined by the overall condition of the person's body. If you wipe and scrape this fat away, the kidney substance will appear uneven and as if it has been eroded. This is not because this part is naturally different from the rest. Rather, it is because of the divisions of the large vessels located there. It cannot appear as continuous and uniform as the substance found in the convex part of the kidneys. That convex area is filled everywhere with extremely thin branches of vessels that almost escape the sight. For this reason, I suspect most anatomists have asserted that the substance of the kidneys is sponge-like and cavernous. After this, consider carefully how that same membrane of the kidney is reflected and expanded. Notice how elegantly and fittingly it receives the branches of the vessels. Indeed, the branches themselves spread out above and below like the toes of a goose, supported by that same membrane.

Cassia is of two kinds: cassia fistula and wood-cassia, which is the fruit of something growing near the borders of Babylon. It has diverse species. One is similar to cinnamon, which is reddish and round and has a solid substance, and when it is broken or ground, it does not bend but resists; it is sharp in taste and a little sweet, and this is what provides the virtue. Another is a species that is bitterish, having partially distinct colors, and it has the virtue of the medium; one must choose that which is not easily broken but bends, and which is of a sharp taste mixed with sweetness and aromaticity, being fragile and distinct with whitish interiors and reddish intermixtures. Sometimes it is adulterated when one adds the bark of capers, and they compel it with a bitterish taste. It has a diuretic virtue, that is, a divisive one because of the subtlety of its substance. It also has the virtue of being taken and applied; furthermore, it has the power of strengthening because of its aromaticity. It cures rheumatism and cold causes; it helps those who are epileptic or have the falling sickness; it strengthens the brain; it purges the kidneys and bladder; it ripens and heals apostemes <note>abscesses or swellings</note>; it de-obstructs the kidneys, liver, and spleen; masticated, it removes or cuts off the stench of the mouth; it provokes menstruation and strengthens the womb; it helps with swooning and defects of the heart if a syrup is made from its powder, roses, and the bone of a stag. Dioscorides and Pliny agree.

### Of Cassia Fistula. Chapter XXVIII
Cassia fistula is the fruit of a certain tree that produces long seeds; in time, it elongates and thickens, and through the action of heat, it ripens. The marrow existing inside is black and humid and sweet, and it is mixed with white signs and separated by certain cells in the manner of a honeycomb. One must choose that which is thick and heavy, which shows much humidity in its being; one must also know it should be light and sonorous, which is if it lacks weight and dryness. By virtue, it has the power of softening, mollifying, and cleansing, and it miraculously mitigates the heat of blood and purifies bile and blood. It dissolves apostemes of the throat; it is useful for the viscera and leads out fatty humor; it removes tumors of the viscera and pains of the intestines when drunk. Dioscorides agrees. To which the authors say, as Ovid in the 15th book of the Metamorphoses: "As soon as the cassia and the light ears of nard, etc." And although Pliny and Persius and others say it everywhere.

### Of Calamus. Chapter XXIX

<column-break/>

Calamus is aromatic and is from the Greek; it is named from the similarity to a visual reed <note>a common reed</note>, as Isidore says in Book 17. It is produced in India with many knotted joints, sweet in scent, fragrant with a wondrous sweetness of odor; when it is broken, it is split and divided into many parts. In taste, it is similar to cassia with a gentle, biting acrimony, as Papias says, and it is of a serving virtue. In the gloss on the Eroticum, it is said that aromatic calamus is a species that grows near Mount Lebanon. Dioscorides says it grows everywhere. Pliny says: It is a species that is hot and dry in the second degree. The root of a certain fruit is very similar to calamus and of great odor, and it has a cavity in the manner of a reed in which wood is found, which it extracts; although it is of no value, sometimes one leaves it, and it seems to be of greater weight. The same authors say calamus is of two kinds, namely, that which strengthens the stomach and aids digestion, and that which acts as a remedy for the womb, similar to wormwood. It helps those with cardiac issues and defects of the heart, which the Greeks call syncope, for which it helps much when added to rose water. Pliny says the calamus of odor is Indian and is of the greatest value; it is reddish, full of knots, and dense, and when it is not broken into many parts, it is very dry and is very medicinal, almost like cassia or even cinnamon. Seek the fruit for it also. For it provokes menstruation.
